The productivity paradox refers to the slowdown in productivity growth in the United States in the 1970s and 1980s despite rapid development in the field of information technology (IT) over the same period. The term was coined by Erik Brynjolfsson in a 1993 paper ("The Productivity Paradox of IT")[1] inspired by a quip by Nobel Laureate Robert Solow "You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics."[2] For this reason, it is also sometimes referred to as the Solow paradox.[3]

The productivity paradox inspired many research efforts at explaining the slowdown, only for the paradox to disappear with renewed productivity growth in the developed countries in the 1990s. However, issues raised by those research efforts remain important in the study of productivity growth in general, and became important again when productivity growth slowed around the world again from the 2000s to the present day. Thus the term "productivity paradox" can also refer to the more general disconnect between powerful computer technologies and weak productivity growth.[4]

1970s to 1980s productivity paradox

[edit]

The 1970s to 1980s productivity paradox has been defined as a perceived "discrepancy between measures of investment in information technology and measures of output at the national level."[5] Brynjolfsson documented that productivity growth slowed down at the level of the whole U.S. economy, and often within individual sectors that had invested heavily in IT, despite dramatic advances in computer power and increasing investment in IT.[1] Similar trends were seen in many other nations.[6] While the computing capacity of the U.S. increased a hundredfold in the 1970s and 1980s,[7] labor productivity growth slowed from over 3% in the 1960s to roughly 1% in the 1980s. This perceived paradox was popularized in the media by analysts such as Steven Roach and later Paul Strassmann.

Many observers disagree that any meaningful "productivity paradox" exists and others, while acknowledging the disconnect between IT capacity and spending, view it less as a paradox than a series of unwarranted assumptions about the impact of technology on productivity. In the latter view, this disconnect is emblematic of our need to understand and do a better job of deploying the technology that becomes available to us rather than an arcane paradox that by its nature is difficult to unravel.

Some point to historical parallels with the steam engine and with electricity, where the dividends of a productivity-enhancing disruptive technology were reaped only slowly, with an initial lag, over the course of decades, due to the time required for the technologies to diffuse into common use, and due to the time required to reorganize around and master efficient use of the new technology.[8][9] As with previous technologies, an extremely large number of initial cutting-edge investments in IT were counterproductive and over-optimistic.[10] Some modest IT-based gains may have been difficult to detect amid the apparent overall slowing of productivity growth, which is generally attributed to one or more of a variety of non-IT factors, such as oil shocks, increased regulation or other cultural changes, a hypothetical decrease in labor quality, a hypothetical exhaustion or slowdown in non-IT innovation, and/or a coincidence of sector-specific problems.[11]

This phenomenon inspired a number of hypothesized explanations of the paradox.

Mismeasurement hypotheses

[edit]

The mismeasurement hypotheses of the productivity paradox center around the idea that real output estimates during this time overestimates inflation and understates productivity, because they do not take into account quality improvements of IT goods and goods in general. The US government measures productivity by comparing real output measurements from period to period, which they do by dividing the nominal output measurements from each period into an inflation component, and a real output component. The US government's calculations of real GDP does not take into account inflation directly, and during the 1970s and 1980s these calculations estimate inflation from observing the change in total spending and change in total units consumed for goods and services over time. This accurately represented inflation if the consumed goods and services in the output measurements remain relatively the same from period to period, but if goods and services improved from period to period the change in spending will characterize consumer spending for quality improvements as inflation, which overstates inflation and under estimates productivity growth. Later calculations of GDP partly compensates for this problem using hedonic regression methods, and these methods estimate that the true price of mainframe computers alone from 1950 to 1980s may have declined more than 20% per year. These estimated implicit price decreases are indications of the scale of productivity growth missing from the output measurements. These measurement issues, as well as measurement issues with new products, continues to affect output and productivity measurement today.[12][1]

Redistribution and dissipation of profits hypotheses

[edit]

The redistribution and dissipation of profits hypotheses rely on the idea that firms might make IT investments that are productive for the firm by capturing more wealth available in their industry, but do not create more wealth in that industry. Some examples of these types of IT investments might be market research, marketing and advertisement investments. These investments help firms compete away market share from firms with less of these IT investments, while they do not improve the total output of the industry as a whole.[1]

Mismanagement of IT hypotheses

[edit]

The mismanagement of IT hypotheses suggests that IT investments are really not productive at a firm level, but that decision makers are making the investments nevertheless. These hypotheses suggest that firm level decision-makers make IT investments regardless of the cost and productivity benefits of the investments because of the difficulty in quantifying IT productivity gains.[1]

IT unproductive hypotheses

[edit]

Other economists have made a more controversial charge against the utility of computers: that they pale into insignificance as a source of productivity advantage when compared to the Industrial Revolution, electrification, infrastructures (canals and waterways, railroads, highway system), Fordist mass production and the replacement of human and animal power with machines.[13] High productivity growth occurred from last decades of the 19th century until the 1973, with a peak from 1929 to 1973, then declined to levels of the early 19th century. [14] [15]

However, the hypothesis that IT was fundamentally unproductive weakened in the early 1990s, as total factor productivity growth in the United States accelerated. From 2000 through the most recent data in 2022, the information technology industry was among those to see the fastest productivity growth.[16]

Gordon J. Bjork points out that manufacturing productivity gains continued, although at a decreasing rate than in decades past; however, the cost reductions in manufacturing shrank the sector size. The services and government sectors, where productivity growth is very low, gained in share, dragging down the overall productivity number. Because government services are priced at cost with no value added, government productivity growth is near zero as an artifact of the way in which it is measured. Bjork also points out that manufacturing uses more capital per unit of output than government or services.[17]

Lags due to learning and adjustment hypothesis

[edit]

The "lags due to learning and adjustment" (lags) hypothesis explains the productivity paradox as the idea that output and productivity gains from investment in IT materializes well after the investment takes place, so any output and productivity observations of the 1970s and 1980s will not observe those gains. Surveys of executives as well as econometric studies indicated that it might take between two and five years for IT investments to have any impact on organizations that made IT investments. The lags in IT benefits might also slow down IT investments, as observations of short-term marginal costs and benefits of IT investments might seem irrational.[1] IT investments might also require complementary capital investments to be made to be fully productive.[8] Because these investments are costly, but do not create measurable benefits until later, they can create a "productivity J-curve".[18] Subsequent observations of productivity increases in 2000s may be due to lag effects of IT investments in the 1970s-1990s period.[19]

End of the 1970s to 1980s productivity paradox

[edit]

By the late 1990s there were some signs that productivity in the workplace had been improved by the introduction of IT, especially in the United States. In fact, Erik Brynjolfsson and his colleagues found a significant positive relationship between IT investments and productivity, at least when these investments were made to complement organizational changes.[20][21][22][23] A large share of the productivity gains outside the IT-equipment industry itself have been in retail, wholesale and finance.[24] The 1990s IT-related productivity jump arguably resolved the original paradox in favor of the lag in productivity benefits explanations.[6][9]

2000 to 2020s productivity slowdown

[edit]

There was an additional slowdown in productivity growth in the United States and developed countries from the 2000s to 2020s; sometimes the newer slowdown is referred to as the productivity slowdown, the productivity puzzle, or the productivity paradox 2.0. The 2000s to 2020s productivity slowdown has been defined in terms of lower developed world productivity growth, especially in the US, in this period compared to the period between 1940s and 1970s, and the period between 1994 and 2004.[25]

New mismeasurement hypotheses

[edit]

New mismeasurement hypotheses are conceptually similar to the 1970s and 1980s mismeasurement hypotheses of the productivity paradox in that they still center around the idea that real output estimates overestimates inflation and understates productivity; however, the new mismeasurement hypotheses looks at additional sources of estimation error like the output effects of adding new, never-before-seen products. As in the 1970s and 1980s, modern, post-2000s US productivity measures are produced by comparing real output measurements from period to period, which they do by dividing the nominal output measurements from each period into an inflation component, and a real output component. As before, the US government's calculations of real GDP do not take into account inflation directly but estimate inflation from observing the change in total spending and change in total units consumed for goods and services over time. These new inflation calculation methods, however, compensate for previously raised mismeasurement problems using hedonic regression methods, but they still do not take into account the output-inflation effects of introducing new products. If existing goods and services improved from period to period, hedonic regression estimates could produce an estimate of what consumers would pay for the quality improvements and lower inflation estimates by those amounts. However, if new goods and services in a sector appear in one time period, the extra money that consumers would pay for creation of those new goods and services are not captured in the inflation estimate; the observed extra spending by consumers in that sector is measured as inflation and not attributed to the new goods and services in this case. Thus, the modern real output calculations will characterize consumer spending for new products and services, as well as any spending for quality improvements not captured by the hedonic regression models, as inflation, which overstates inflation and underestimates productivity growth.[26][1]

New lag hypotheses are substantially the same as older lag hypotheses but focus on the lag effects of different new technology and different ways that technology can improve productivity. Productivity benefits from IT investments in the mid-1990s tend to come from their ability to improve supply-chain, back-office and end-to-end operations. Productivity benefits from IT investments post-2000s are expected to come from front-office operations and new product introductions.[27]

Little productivity benefit from IT in manufacturing

[edit]

A study by Acemoglu, Autor, Dorn, Hanson, and Price (2014) examined the productivity benefits of information technology within the manufacturing sector. The researchers concluded that:

There is... Little evidence of faster productivity growth in IT-intensive industries after the late 1990s. Second and more importantly, to the extent that there is more rapid growth of labor productivity... This is associated with declining output... And even more rapidly declining employment.

— [28], Acemoglu et al. (2014)

This empirical evidence indicates that in certain industrial contexts, observed increases in labor productivity may not reflect an expansion in total output, but rather a contraction of the workforce. This trend is mirrored in other high-tech sectors. For example, it is estimated that up to half of the growth in U.S. healthcare spending can be attributed directly to rising technology costs.[29]

Despite high expectations for online retail sales, individual item and small quantity handling and transportation costs may offset the savings of not having to maintain bricks and mortar stores.[30] Online retail sales has proven successful in specialty items, collectibles and higher priced goods. Some airline and hotel retailers and aggregators have also witnessed great success.

Online commerce has been extremely successful in banking, airline, hotel, and rental car reservations, to name a few.

blocks.html_en: The productivity paradox refers to the slowdown in productivity growth in the United States in the 1970s and 1980s despite rapid development in the field of information technology (IT) over the same period. The term was coined by Erik Brynjolfsson in a 1993 paper ("The Productivity Paradox of IT")[1] inspired by a quip by Nobel Laureate Robert Solow "You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics."[2] For this reason, it is also sometimes referred to as the Solow paradox.[3]

sentences.en: The productivity paradox refers to the slowdown in productivity growth in the United States in the 1970s and 1980s despite rapid development in the field of information technology (IT) over the same period.
sentences.zh: 生产率悖论是指美国在20世纪70年代和1980年代，尽管信息技术（IT）领域快速发展，但生产率增长却放缓。

sentences.en: The term was coined by Erik Brynjolfsson in a 1993 paper ("The Productivity Paradox of IT")[1] inspired by a quip by Nobel Laureate Robert Solow "You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics."[2] For this reason, it is also sometimes referred to as the Solow paradox.[3]
sentences.zh: 该术语是由 Erik Brynjolfsson 在 1993 年的一篇论文（“IT 生产力悖论”）[1] 中创造的，其灵感来自诺贝尔奖获得者罗伯特·索洛 (Robert Solow) 的俏皮话“你可以在任何地方看到计算机时代，但只能在生产力统计数据中看到。”[2] 因此，它有时也被称为索洛悖论。 [3]

blocks.html_en: The productivity paradox inspired many research efforts at explaining the slowdown, only for the paradox to disappear with renewed productivity growth in the developed countries in the 1990s. However, issues raised by those research efforts remain important in the study of productivity growth in general, and became important again when productivity growth slowed around the world again from the 2000s to the present day. Thus the term "productivity paradox" can also refer to the more general disconnect between powerful computer technologies and weak productivity growth.[4]

sentences.en: The productivity paradox inspired many research efforts at explaining the slowdown, only for the paradox to disappear with renewed productivity growth in the developed countries in the 1990s.
sentences.zh: 生产率悖论激发了许多研究努力来解释经济放缓，但随着 20 世纪 90 年代发达国家生产率的重新增长，这一悖论就消失了。

sentences.en: However, issues raised by those research efforts remain important in the study of productivity growth in general, and became important again when productivity growth slowed around the world again from the 2000s to the present day.
sentences.zh: 然而，这些研究工作提出的问题在总体生产率增长研究中仍然很重要，并且当全球生产率增长从 2000 年代至今再次放缓时，这些问题再次变得重要。

sentences.en: Thus the term "productivity paradox" can also refer to the more general disconnect between powerful computer technologies and weak productivity growth.[4]
sentences.zh: 因此，“生产力悖论”一词也可以指强大的计算机技术与疲软的生产力增长之间更普遍的脱节。 [4]

blocks.html_en: 1970s to 1980s productivity paradox

sentences.zh: 20 世纪 70 年代至 80 年代的生产力悖论

blocks.html_en: [edit]

The 1970s to 1980s productivity paradox has been defined as a perceived "discrepancy between measures of investment in information technology and measures of output at the national level."[5] Brynjolfsson documented that productivity growth slowed down at the level of the whole U.S. economy, and often within individual sectors that had invested heavily in IT, despite dramatic advances in computer power and increasing investment in IT.[1] Similar trends were seen in many other nations.[6] While the computing capacity of the U.S. increased a hundredfold in the 1970s and 1980s,[7] labor productivity growth slowed from over 3% in the 1960s to roughly 1% in the 1980s. This perceived paradox was popularized in the media by analysts such as Steven Roach and later Paul Strassmann.

sentences.en: The 1970s to 1980s productivity paradox has been defined as a perceived "discrepancy between measures of investment in information technology and measures of output at the national level."[5] Brynjolfsson documented that productivity growth slowed down at the level of the whole U.S. economy, and often within individual sectors that had invested heavily in IT, despite dramatic advances in computer power and increasing investment in IT.[1] Similar trends were seen in many other nations.[6] While the computing capacity of the U.S. increased a hundredfold in the 1970s and 1980s,[7] labor productivity growth slowed from over 3% in the 1960s to roughly 1% in the 1980s.
sentences.zh: 1970 年代至 1980 年代的生产力悖论被定义为一种明显的“信息技术投资衡量标准与国家层面产出衡量标准之间的差异。”[5] Brynjolfsson 记录道，尽管计算机能力取得了巨大进步并且 IT 投资不断增加，但整个美国经济层面的生产力增长放缓，而且往往是在 IT 领域投入巨资的个别部门。[1]许多其他国家也出现了类似的趋势。[6]尽管美国的计算能力在 20 世纪 70 年代和 1980 年代增长了数百倍，[7] 劳动生产率增长却从 1960 年代的 3% 以上放缓至 1980 年代的约 1%。

sentences.en: This perceived paradox was popularized in the media by analysts such as Steven Roach and later Paul Strassmann.
sentences.zh: 史蒂文·罗奇（Steven Roach）和后来的保罗·斯特拉斯曼（Paul Strassmann）等分析师在媒体上宣传了这种悖论。

blocks.html_en: Many observers disagree that any meaningful "productivity paradox" exists and others, while acknowledging the disconnect between IT capacity and spending, view it less as a paradox than a series of unwarranted assumptions about the impact of technology on productivity. In the latter view, this disconnect is emblematic of our need to understand and do a better job of deploying the technology that becomes available to us rather than an arcane paradox that by its nature is difficult to unravel.

sentences.en: Many observers disagree that any meaningful "productivity paradox" exists and others, while acknowledging the disconnect between IT capacity and spending, view it less as a paradox than a series of unwarranted assumptions about the impact of technology on productivity.
sentences.zh: 许多观察家不认为存在任何有意义的“生产力悖论”，而其他人虽然承认 IT 能力与支出之间存在脱节，但与其说这是一个悖论，不如说是对技术对生产力影响的一系列毫无根据的假设。

sentences.en: In the latter view, this disconnect is emblematic of our need to understand and do a better job of deploying the technology that becomes available to us rather than an arcane paradox that by its nature is difficult to unravel.
sentences.zh: 在后一种观点中，这种脱节象征着我们需要理解并更好地部署我们可用的技术，而不是一个本质上难以解开的神秘悖论。

blocks.html_en: Some point to historical parallels with the steam engine and with electricity, where the dividends of a productivity-enhancing disruptive technology were reaped only slowly, with an initial lag, over the course of decades, due to the time required for the technologies to diffuse into common use, and due to the time required to reorganize around and master efficient use of the new technology.[8][9] As with previous technologies, an extremely large number of initial cutting-edge investments in IT were counterproductive and over-optimistic.[10] Some modest IT-based gains may have been difficult to detect amid the apparent overall slowing of productivity growth, which is generally attributed to one or more of a variety of non-IT factors, such as oil shocks, increased regulation or other cultural changes, a hypothetical decrease in labor quality, a hypothetical exhaustion or slowdown in non-IT innovation, and/or a coincidence of sector-specific problems.[11]

sentences.en: Some point to historical parallels with the steam engine and with electricity, where the dividends of a productivity-enhancing disruptive technology were reaped only slowly, with an initial lag, over the course of decades, due to the time required for the technologies to diffuse into common use, and due to the time required to reorganize around and master efficient use of the new technology.[8][9] As with previous technologies, an extremely large number of initial cutting-edge investments in IT were counterproductive and over-optimistic.[10] Some modest IT-based gains may have been difficult to detect amid the apparent overall slowing of productivity growth, which is generally attributed to one or more of a variety of non-IT factors, such as oil shocks, increased regulation or other cultural changes, a hypothetical decrease in labor quality, a hypothetical exhaustion or slowdown in non-IT innovation, and/or a coincidence of sector-specific problems.[11]
sentences.zh: 一些人指出，蒸汽机和电力在历史上有相似之处，提高生产力的颠覆性技术的红利是在数十年的时间里缓慢地获得的，最初存在滞后，因为这些技术需要时间才能扩散到普遍使用，并且需要时间来重新组织和掌握新技术的有效使用。 [8][9]与以前的技术一样，IT 领域的大量初始尖端投资适得其反且过于乐观。 [10]在生产率增长明显总体放缓的情况下，一些基于信息技术的适度收益可能很难被发现，这通常归因于一种或多种非信息技术因素，例如石油冲击、监管加强或其他文化变化、假设的劳动力质量下降、假设的非信息技术创新枯竭或放缓，和/或特定部门问题的巧合。 [11]

blocks.html_en: This phenomenon inspired a number of hypothesized explanations of the paradox.

sentences.en: This phenomenon inspired a number of hypothesized explanations of the paradox.
sentences.zh: 这种现象激发了对该悖论的许多假设解释。

blocks.html_en: Mismeasurement hypotheses

sentences.zh: 误测假设

blocks.html_en: [edit]

The mismeasurement hypotheses of the productivity paradox center around the idea that real output estimates during this time overestimates inflation and understates productivity, because they do not take into account quality improvements of IT goods and goods in general. The US government measures productivity by comparing real output measurements from period to period, which they do by dividing the nominal output measurements from each period into an inflation component, and a real output component. The US government's calculations of real GDP does not take into account inflation directly, and during the 1970s and 1980s these calculations estimate inflation from observing the change in total spending and change in total units consumed for goods and services over time. This accurately represented inflation if the consumed goods and services in the output measurements remain relatively the same from period to period, but if goods and services improved from period to period the change in spending will characterize consumer spending for quality improvements as inflation, which overstates inflation and under estimates productivity growth. Later calculations of GDP partly compensates for this problem using hedonic regression methods, and these methods estimate that the true price of mainframe computers alone from 1950 to 1980s may have declined more than 20% per year. These estimated implicit price decreases are indications of the scale of productivity growth missing from the output measurements. These measurement issues, as well as measurement issues with new products, continues to affect output and productivity measurement today.[12][1]

sentences.en: The mismeasurement hypotheses of the productivity paradox center around the idea that real output estimates during this time overestimates inflation and understates productivity, because they do not take into account quality improvements of IT goods and goods in general.
sentences.zh: 生产率悖论的误测假设集中在这样一种观点上：这一时期的实际产出估计高估了通货膨胀并低估了生产率，因为它们没有考虑到 IT 商品和一般商品的质量改进。

sentences.en: The US government measures productivity by comparing real output measurements from period to period, which they do by dividing the nominal output measurements from each period into an inflation component, and a real output component.
sentences.zh: 美国政府通过比较不同时期的实际产出测量来衡量生产率，他们通过将每个时期的名义产出测量划分为通货膨胀部分和实际产出部分来实现这一点。

sentences.en: The US government's calculations of real GDP does not take into account inflation directly, and during the 1970s and 1980s these calculations estimate inflation from observing the change in total spending and change in total units consumed for goods and services over time.
sentences.zh: 美国政府对实际GDP的计算并不直接考虑通货膨胀，在20世纪70年代和1980年代，这些计算通过观察总支出的变化以及商品和服务消耗的总单位随时间的变化来估计通货膨胀。

sentences.en: This accurately represented inflation if the consumed goods and services in the output measurements remain relatively the same from period to period, but if goods and services improved from period to period the change in spending will characterize consumer spending for quality improvements as inflation, which overstates inflation and under estimates productivity growth.
sentences.zh: 如果产出测量中的消费商品和服务在不同时期保持相对相同，则这准确地代表了通货膨胀，但如果商品和服务在不同时期有所改善，则支出的变化将把用于质量改进的消费者支出描述为通货膨胀，从而高估了通货膨胀并低估了生产率增长。

sentences.en: Later calculations of GDP partly compensates for this problem using hedonic regression methods, and these methods estimate that the true price of mainframe computers alone from 1950 to 1980s may have declined more than 20% per year.
sentences.zh: 后来的 GDP 计算使用特征回归方法部分补偿了这个问题，这些方法估计，从 1950 年代到 1980 年代，仅大型计算机的真实价格就可能每年下降 20% 以上。

sentences.en: These estimated implicit price decreases are indications of the scale of productivity growth missing from the output measurements.
sentences.zh: 这些估计的隐性价格下降表明了产出测量中缺少的生产率增长规模。

sentences.en: These measurement issues, as well as measurement issues with new products, continues to affect output and productivity measurement today.[12][1]
sentences.zh: 这些测量问题以及新产品的测量问题继续影响着当今的产出和生产率测量。[12][1]

blocks.html_en: Redistribution and dissipation of profits hypotheses

sentences.en: Redistribution and dissipation of profits hypotheses
sentences.zh: 利润再分配和耗散假设

blocks.html_en: [edit]

The redistribution and dissipation of profits hypotheses rely on the idea that firms might make IT investments that are productive for the firm by capturing more wealth available in their industry, but do not create more wealth in that industry. Some examples of these types of IT investments might be market research, marketing and advertisement investments. These investments help firms compete away market share from firms with less of these IT investments, while they do not improve the total output of the industry as a whole.[1]

sentences.en: The redistribution and dissipation of profits hypotheses rely on the idea that firms might make IT investments that are productive for the firm by capturing more wealth available in their industry, but do not create more wealth in that industry.
sentences.zh: 利润再分配和耗散假设依赖于这样一种观点：企业可能会通过获取行业中更多的可用财富来进行对企业有利的 IT 投资，但不会在该行业中创造更多的财富。

sentences.en: Some examples of these types of IT investments might be market research, marketing and advertisement investments.
sentences.zh: 这些类型的 IT 投资的一些例子可能是市场研究、营销和广告投资。

sentences.en: These investments help firms compete away market share from firms with less of these IT investments, while they do not improve the total output of the industry as a whole.[1]
sentences.zh: 这些投资帮助企业从 IT 投资较少的企业手中夺取市场份额，但并没有提高整个行业的总产出。 [1]

blocks.html_en: Mismanagement of IT hypotheses

sentences.zh: IT 假设管理不善

blocks.html_en: [edit]

The mismanagement of IT hypotheses suggests that IT investments are really not productive at a firm level, but that decision makers are making the investments nevertheless. These hypotheses suggest that firm level decision-makers make IT investments regardless of the cost and productivity benefits of the investments because of the difficulty in quantifying IT productivity gains.[1]

sentences.en: The mismanagement of IT hypotheses suggests that IT investments are really not productive at a firm level, but that decision makers are making the investments nevertheless.
sentences.zh: IT 假设的管理不善表明，IT 投资在公司层面实际上并没有什么成效，但决策者仍然在进行投资。

sentences.en: These hypotheses suggest that firm level decision-makers make IT investments regardless of the cost and productivity benefits of the investments because of the difficulty in quantifying IT productivity gains.[1]
sentences.zh: 这些假设表明，由于难以量化 IT 生产力收益，公司级决策者在进行 IT 投资时不考虑投资的成本和生产力收益。 [1]

blocks.html_en: IT unproductive hypotheses

sentences.zh: IT 无效假设

blocks.html_en: [edit]

Other economists have made a more controversial charge against the utility of computers: that they pale into insignificance as a source of productivity advantage when compared to the Industrial Revolution, electrification, infrastructures (canals and waterways, railroads, highway system), Fordist mass production and the replacement of human and animal power with machines.[13] High productivity growth occurred from last decades of the 19th century until the 1973, with a peak from 1929 to 1973, then declined to levels of the early 19th century. [14] [15]

sentences.en: Other economists have made a more controversial charge against the utility of computers: that they pale into insignificance as a source of productivity advantage when compared to the Industrial Revolution, electrification, infrastructures (canals and waterways, railroads, highway system), Fordist mass production and the replacement of human and animal power with machines.[13] High productivity growth occurred from last decades of the 19th century until the 1973, with a peak from 1929 to 1973, then declined to levels of the early 19th century. [14] [15]
sentences.zh: 其他经济学家对计算机的效用提出了更具争议性的指控：与工业革命、电气化、基础设施（运河和水道、铁路、高速公路系统）、福特主义大规模生产以及用机器取代人力和畜力相比，计算机作为生产力优势的来源显得微不足道。 [13]生产率的高增长发生在 19 世纪最后几十年到 1973 年，1929 年到 1973 年达到顶峰，然后下降到 19 世纪初的水平。 [14][15]

blocks.html_en: However, the hypothesis that IT was fundamentally unproductive weakened in the early 1990s, as total factor productivity growth in the United States accelerated. From 2000 through the most recent data in 2022, the information technology industry was among those to see the fastest productivity growth.[16]

sentences.en: However, the hypothesis that IT was fundamentally unproductive weakened in the early 1990s, as total factor productivity growth in the United States accelerated.
sentences.zh: 然而，随着美国全要素生产率的加速增长，关于 IT 根本上没有生产力的假设在 20 世纪 90 年代初被削弱。

sentences.en: From 2000 through the most recent data in 2022, the information technology industry was among those to see the fastest productivity growth.[16]
sentences.zh: 从 2000 年到 2022 年的最新数据，信息技术行业是生产率增长最快的行业之一。 [16]

blocks.html_en: Gordon J. Bjork points out that manufacturing productivity gains continued, although at a decreasing rate than in decades past; however, the cost reductions in manufacturing shrank the sector size. The services and government sectors, where productivity growth is very low, gained in share, dragging down the overall productivity number. Because government services are priced at cost with no value added, government productivity growth is near zero as an artifact of the way in which it is measured. Bjork also points out that manufacturing uses more capital per unit of output than government or services.[17]

sentences.zh: 比约克指出，制造业生产率持续提高，尽管增速比过去几十年有所下降。然而，制造业成本的降低缩小了行业规模。

sentences.en: The services and government sectors, where productivity growth is very low, gained in share, dragging down the overall productivity number.

blocks.html_en: Lags due to learning and adjustment hypothesis

sentences.en: Lags due to learning and adjustment hypothesis
sentences.zh: 由于学习和调整假设而滞后

blocks.html_en: [edit]

The "lags due to learning and adjustment" (lags) hypothesis explains the productivity paradox as the idea that output and productivity gains from investment in IT materializes well after the investment takes place, so any output and productivity observations of the 1970s and 1980s will not observe those gains. Surveys of executives as well as econometric studies indicated that it might take between two and five years for IT investments to have any impact on organizations that made IT investments. The lags in IT benefits might also slow down IT investments, as observations of short-term marginal costs and benefits of IT investments might seem irrational.[1] IT investments might also require complementary capital investments to be made to be fully productive.[8] Because these investments are costly, but do not create measurable benefits until later, they can create a "productivity J-curve".[18] Subsequent observations of productivity increases in 2000s may be due to lag effects of IT investments in the 1970s-1990s period.[19]

sentences.en: The "lags due to learning and adjustment" (lags) hypothesis explains the productivity paradox as the idea that output and productivity gains from investment in IT materializes well after the investment takes place, so any output and productivity observations of the 1970s and 1980s will not observe those gains.

blocks.html_en: End of the 1970s to 1980s productivity paradox

sentences.en: End of the 1970s to 1980s productivity paradox

blocks.html_en: [edit]

By the late 1990s there were some signs that productivity in the workplace had been improved by the introduction of IT, especially in the United States. In fact, Erik Brynjolfsson and his colleagues found a significant positive relationship between IT investments and productivity, at least when these investments were made to complement organizational changes.[20][21][22][23] A large share of the productivity gains outside the IT-equipment industry itself have been in retail, wholesale and finance.[24] The 1990s IT-related productivity jump arguably resolved the original paradox in favor of the lag in productivity benefits explanations.[6][9]

sentences.zh: 到 20 世纪 90 年代末，有一些迹象表明，工作场所的生产力因 IT 的引入而得到提高，尤其是在美国。

sentences.en: In fact, Erik Brynjolfsson and his colleagues found a significant positive relationship between IT investments and productivity, at least when these investments were made to complement organizational changes.[20][21][22][23] A large share of the productivity gains outside the IT-equipment industry itself have been in retail, wholesale and finance.[24] The 1990s IT-related productivity jump arguably resolved the original paradox in favor of the lag in productivity benefits explanations.[6][9]
sentences.zh: 事实上，Erik Brynjolfsson 和他的同事发现 IT 投资和生产力之间存在显着的正相关关系，至少当这些投资是为了补充组织变革时是如此。[20][21][22][23] IT 设备行业本身之外的生产率增长的很大一部分来自于零售、批发和金融行业。 [24] 20 世纪 90 年代与 IT 相关的生产力跃升可以说解决了最初的悖论，有利于生产力效益滞后的解释。 [6][9]

blocks.html_en: 2000 to 2020s productivity slowdown

sentences.zh: 2000年至2020年代生产力放缓

blocks.html_en: [edit]

There was an additional slowdown in productivity growth in the United States and developed countries from the 2000s to 2020s; sometimes the newer slowdown is referred to as the productivity slowdown, the productivity puzzle, or the productivity paradox 2.0. The 2000s to 2020s productivity slowdown has been defined in terms of lower developed world productivity growth, especially in the US, in this period compared to the period between 1940s and 1970s, and the period between 1994 and 2004.[25]

blocks.html_en: New mismeasurement hypotheses

sentences.zh: 新的误测假设

blocks.html_en: [edit]

New mismeasurement hypotheses are conceptually similar to the 1970s and 1980s mismeasurement hypotheses of the productivity paradox in that they still center around the idea that real output estimates overestimates inflation and understates productivity; however, the new mismeasurement hypotheses looks at additional sources of estimation error like the output effects of adding new, never-before-seen products. As in the 1970s and 1980s, modern, post-2000s US productivity measures are produced by comparing real output measurements from period to period, which they do by dividing the nominal output measurements from each period into an inflation component, and a real output component. As before, the US government's calculations of real GDP do not take into account inflation directly but estimate inflation from observing the change in total spending and change in total units consumed for goods and services over time. These new inflation calculation methods, however, compensate for previously raised mismeasurement problems using hedonic regression methods, but they still do not take into account the output-inflation effects of introducing new products. If existing goods and services improved from period to period, hedonic regression estimates could produce an estimate of what consumers would pay for the quality improvements and lower inflation estimates by those amounts. However, if new goods and services in a sector appear in one time period, the extra money that consumers would pay for creation of those new goods and services are not captured in the inflation estimate; the observed extra spending by consumers in that sector is measured as inflation and not attributed to the new goods and services in this case. Thus, the modern real output calculations will characterize consumer spending for new products and services, as well as any spending for quality improvements not captured by the hedonic regression models, as inflation, which overstates inflation and underestimates productivity growth.[26][1]

content_html_zh:
生产率悖论是指美国在20世纪70年代和1980年代，尽管信息技术（IT）领域快速发展，但生产率增长却放缓。 该术语是由 Erik Brynjolfsson 在 1993 年的一篇论文（“IT 生产力悖论”）[1] 中创造的，其灵感来自诺贝尔奖获得者罗伯特·索洛 (Robert Solow) 的俏皮话“你可以在任何地方看到计算机时代，但只能在生产力统计数据中看到。”[2] 因此，它有时也被称为索洛悖论。 [3]

生产率悖论激发了许多研究努力来解释经济放缓，但随着 20 世纪 90 年代发达国家生产率的重新增长，这一悖论就消失了。 然而，这些研究工作提出的问题在总体生产率增长研究中仍然很重要，并且当全球生产率增长从 2000 年代至今再次放缓时，这些问题再次变得重要。 因此，“生产力悖论”一词也可以指强大的计算机技术与疲软的生产力增长之间更普遍的脱节。 [4]

20 世纪 70 年代至 80 年代的生产力悖论

[edit]

1970 年代至 1980 年代的生产力悖论被定义为一种明显的“信息技术投资衡量标准与国家层面产出衡量标准之间的差异。”[5] Brynjolfsson 记录道，尽管计算机能力取得了巨大进步并且 IT 投资不断增加，但整个美国经济层面的生产力增长放缓，而且往往是在 IT 领域投入巨资的个别部门。[1]许多其他国家也出现了类似的趋势。[6]尽管美国的计算能力在 20 世纪 70 年代和 1980 年代增长了数百倍，[7] 劳动生产率增长却从 1960 年代的 3% 以上放缓至 1980 年代的约 1%。 史蒂文·罗奇（Steven Roach）和后来的保罗·斯特拉斯曼（Paul Strassmann）等分析师在媒体上宣传了这种悖论。

许多观察家不认为存在任何有意义的“生产力悖论”，而其他人虽然承认 IT 能力与支出之间存在脱节，但与其说这是一个悖论，不如说是对技术对生产力影响的一系列毫无根据的假设。 在后一种观点中，这种脱节象征着我们需要理解并更好地部署我们可用的技术，而不是一个本质上难以解开的神秘悖论。

一些人指出，蒸汽机和电力在历史上有相似之处，提高生产力的颠覆性技术的红利是在数十年的时间里缓慢地获得的，最初存在滞后，因为这些技术需要时间才能扩散到普遍使用，并且需要时间来重新组织和掌握新技术的有效使用。 [8][9]与以前的技术一样，IT 领域的大量初始尖端投资适得其反且过于乐观。 [10]在生产率增长明显总体放缓的情况下，一些基于信息技术的适度收益可能很难被发现，这通常归因于一种或多种非信息技术因素，例如石油冲击、监管加强或其他文化变化、假设的劳动力质量下降、假设的非信息技术创新枯竭或放缓，和/或特定部门问题的巧合。 [11]

这种现象激发了对该悖论的许多假设解释。

误测假设

[edit]

生产率悖论的误测假设集中在这样一种观点上：这一时期的实际产出估计高估了通货膨胀并低估了生产率，因为它们没有考虑到 IT 商品和一般商品的质量改进。 美国政府通过比较不同时期的实际产出测量来衡量生产率，他们通过将每个时期的名义产出测量划分为通货膨胀部分和实际产出部分来实现这一点。 美国政府对实际GDP的计算并不直接考虑通货膨胀，在20世纪70年代和1980年代，这些计算通过观察总支出的变化以及商品和服务消耗的总单位随时间的变化来估计通货膨胀。 如果产出测量中的消费商品和服务在不同时期保持相对相同，则这准确地代表了通货膨胀，但如果商品和服务在不同时期有所改善，则支出的变化将把用于质量改进的消费者支出描述为通货膨胀，从而高估了通货膨胀并低估了生产率增长。 后来的 GDP 计算使用特征回归方法部分补偿了这个问题，这些方法估计，从 1950 年代到 1980 年代，仅大型计算机的真实价格就可能每年下降 20% 以上。 这些估计的隐性价格下降表明了产出测量中缺少的生产率增长规模。 这些测量问题以及新产品的测量问题继续影响着当今的产出和生产率测量。[12][1]

利润再分配和耗散假设

[edit]

利润再分配和耗散假设依赖于这样一种观点：企业可能会通过获取行业中更多的可用财富来进行对企业有利的 IT 投资，但不会在该行业中创造更多的财富。 这些类型的 IT 投资的一些例子可能是市场研究、营销和广告投资。 这些投资帮助企业从 IT 投资较少的企业手中夺取市场份额，但并没有提高整个行业的总产出。 [1]

IT 假设管理不善

[edit]

IT 假设的管理不善表明，IT 投资在公司层面实际上并没有什么成效，但决策者仍然在进行投资。 这些假设表明，由于难以量化 IT 生产力收益，公司级决策者在进行 IT 投资时不考虑投资的成本和生产力收益。 [1]

IT 无效假设

[edit]

其他经济学家对计算机的效用提出了更具争议性的指控：与工业革命、电气化、基础设施（运河和水道、铁路、高速公路系统）、福特主义大规模生产以及用机器取代人力和畜力相比，计算机作为生产力优势的来源显得微不足道。 [13]生产率的高增长发生在 19 世纪最后几十年到 1973 年，1929 年到 1973 年达到顶峰，然后下降到 19 世纪初的水平。 [14][15]

然而，随着美国全要素生产率的加速增长，关于 IT 根本上没有生产力的假设在 20 世纪 90 年代初被削弱。 从 2000 年到 2022 年的最新数据，信息技术行业是生产率增长最快的行业之一。 [16]

戈登·J。 比约克指出，制造业生产率持续提高，尽管增速比过去几十年有所下降。然而，制造业成本的降低缩小了行业规模。 生产率增长非常低的服务业和政府部门的份额增加，拖累了整体生产率。 由于政府服务按成本定价，没有附加值，因此政府生产率增长接近于零，这是衡量方式的结果。 比约克还指出，制造业每单位产出使用的资本比政府或服务业更多。 [17]

由于学习和调整假设而滞后

[edit]

“学习和调整导致的滞后”（滞后）假说将生产力悖论解释为这样的观点：IT 投资带来的产出和生产力收益在投资发生后很久才会实现，因此对 1970 年代和 1980 年代的任何产出和生产力观察都不会观察到这些收益。 对高管的调查以及计量经济学研究表明，IT 投资可能需要两到五年的时间才能对进行 IT 投资的组织产生影响。 IT 效益的滞后也可能会减缓 IT 投资的速度，因为对 IT 投资的短期边际成本和效益的观察可能看起来不合理。 [1] IT 投资可能还需要补充资本投资才能充分发挥生产力。 [8]因为这些投资成本高昂，但直到后来才能创造可衡量的效益，因此它们可以创建“生产率 J 曲线”。 [18]随后对 2000 年代生产力增长的观察可能是由于 1970 年代至 1990 年代 IT 投资的滞后效应。 [19]

20 世纪 70 年代末至 80 年代的生产力悖论

[edit]

到 20 世纪 90 年代末，有一些迹象表明，工作场所的生产力因 IT 的引入而得到提高，尤其是在美国。 事实上，Erik Brynjolfsson 和他的同事发现 IT 投资和生产力之间存在显着的正相关关系，至少当这些投资是为了补充组织变革时是如此。[20][21][22][23] IT 设备行业本身之外的生产率增长的很大一部分来自于零售、批发和金融行业。 [24] 20 世纪 90 年代与 IT 相关的生产力跃升可以说解决了最初的悖论，有利于生产力效益滞后的解释。 [6][9]

2000年至2020年代生产力放缓

[edit]

从2000年代到2020年代，美国和发达国家的生产率增长进一步放缓；有时，新的放缓被称为生产力放缓、生产力难题或生产力悖论2.0。 2000年代至2020年代的生产率放缓是指与1940年代至1970年代以及1994至2004年间相比，发达国家（尤其是美国）生产率增长较低。 [25]

新的误测假设

[edit]

新的误测假说在概念上与 20 世纪 70 年代和 80 年代的生产率悖论误测假说类似，因为它们仍然围绕着实际产出估计高估通货膨胀并低估生产率的观点；然而，新的误测假设着眼于估计误差的其他来源，例如添加新的、从未见过的产品的产出影响。 与 20 世纪 70 年代和 1980 年代一样，2000 年代后的现代美国生产率指标是通过比较各个时期的实际产出指标来得出的，即通过将每个时期的名义产出指标划分为通货膨胀部分和实际产出部分来实现这一点。 和以前一样，美国政府对实际GDP的计算并不直接考虑通货膨胀，而是通过观察总支出以及商品和服务消费总单位随时间的变化来估计通货膨胀。 然而，这些新的通胀计算方法利用特征回归方法弥补了之前提出的误测问题，但它们仍然没有考虑引入新产品的产出通胀效应。 如果现有的商品和服务随着时间的推移而改善，特征回归估计可以得出消费者愿意为质量改进支付的费用的估计，并根据这些金额降低通货膨胀估计。 然而，如果某个部门在一个时期内出现新的商品和服务，那么消费者为创造这些新商品和服务而支付的额外资金不会计入通货膨胀估计中；在该情况下，观察到的消费者在该部门的额外支出被视为通货膨胀，而不是归因于新商品和服务。 因此，现代实际产出计算将把消费者对新产品和服务的支出，以及特征回归模型未捕获的任何质量改进支出描述为通货膨胀，这夸大了通货膨胀并低估了生产率增长。 [26][1]

新的滞后假设与旧的滞后假设基本相同，但重点关注不同新技术的滞后效应以及技术提高生产率的不同方式。 20 世纪 90 年代中期 IT 投资带来的生产力优势往往来自于改善供应链、后台和端到端运营的能力。 2000 年代后 IT 投资带来的生产力效益预计将来自前台运营和新产品推出。[27]

制造业中的 IT 几乎没有提高生产力

[edit]

Acemoglu、Autor、Dorn、Hanson 和 Price (2014) 的一项研究考察了信息技术在制造业中的生产力优势。 研究人员得出结论：

有... 20 世纪 90 年代后期之后，几乎没有证据表明 IT 密集型行业的生产率增长更快。 其次，也是更重要的一点是，劳动生产率的增长更加迅速…… 这与产量下降有关... 就业下降速度甚至更快。

- [28]，Acemoglu 等人。 (2014)

这一经验证据表明，在某些工业环境中，观察到的劳动生产率的提高可能并不反映总产出的扩张，而是反映了劳动力的收缩。 这一趋势也反映在其他高科技领域。 例如，据估计，美国医疗保健支出增长的一半可直接归因于技术成本的上升。 [29]

尽管对在线零售销售抱有很高的期望，但单个商品和小批量的处理和运输成本可能会抵消无需维护实体店而节省的费用。 [30]事实证明，网上零售在特色商品、收藏品和高价商品方面取得了成功。 一些航空公司和酒店零售商和聚合商也取得了巨大成功。

在线商务在银行、航空公司、酒店和租车预订等领域取得了巨大成功。
